questions.q: What makes an AI system's security surface wider than a traditional application's, per the lesson?
options: The model itself is both a sensitive asset that can be stolen and an attack surface that can be manipulated through its inputs
AI systems never run on real servers
AI systems are immune to normal software vulnerabilities
AI systems don't process any data at all
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that the model adds a new risk category on top of normal application security: it's a stealable asset and a manipulable decision surface at once.

questions.q: What is 'model extraction,' as defined in the lesson?
options: An attacker reconstructing a close approximation of a deployed model by querying it repeatedly
The routine process of exporting a model file for backup purposes
Removing a model from a registry after it's deprecated
A legal process for transferring model ownership between companies
questions.explain: Model extraction is specifically the attack of rebuilding a model's behavior through repeated queries, not a routine export or deprecation process.

questions.q: Why is Python's pickle format called out as a real, specific security risk for model files?
options: Because loading a pickle file executes arbitrary code embedded in it, so a malicious file can run anything on the machine that loads it
Because pickle files are always larger than other formats
Because pickle is incompatible with all machine learning frameworks
Because pickle files cannot be version-controlled
questions.explain: This is the lesson's real, documented example: pickle's deserialization executes code, which is a genuine, well-known security issue with the format.

questions.q: What does the safetensors format do differently from pickle, according to the lesson?
options: It only reads declared tensor data when loading a model, and never executes code
It encrypts all model weights by default
It automatically retrains the model on load
It is only usable for text data, not model weights
questions.explain: safetensors was designed specifically to avoid pickle's code-execution risk by restricting loading to reading declared tensor data only.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in the lesson as a baseline control against the AI-specific risks it covers?
options: Rate limiting and monitoring on inference endpoints to slow down model extraction attempts
Removing all documentation so attackers can't learn about the model
Allowing unrestricted public access to model weights for transparency
Disabling all logging on the inference endpoint
questions.explain: Rate limiting and monitoring inference endpoints is explicitly listed as a baseline control, since extraction requires many repeated queries.
